prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its glucose-dependent insulinotropic action, which made possible incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots rank GLP-1 first, but I do not treat that as the argument. The argument is the arc: proglucagon processing and the identification of GLP-1(7-36) as the bioactive, glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide, then human physiology of secretion and action, then receptor biology and the therapeutic concept, leading to drugs with confirmed effects on glycaemia, body weight and, in large outcome trials, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. The mechanism is clear, the work is more than two decades old and independently replicated, and the clinical scale makes delay hard to justify. As a neurologist I also note the central appetite-regulating action, which is why the discovery reaches beyond endocrinology. Holst, Drucker and Mojsov are the three discovery-side scientists in the credited list that best represent the physiological finding.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The credited list has four names, Habener is absent, and Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested in the field. Leaving out Knudsen, whose long-acting analogue design produced liraglutide and semaglutide, risks honouring the biology while omitting the step that made it a medicine, and a three-person cap cannot fix that. A secondary concern is that the citation could be read as a physiology prize while the public impact is in drugs, so the wording must be careful. I cannot settle the priority question from the supplied evidence and I should not pretend otherwise.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that Mojsov's contribution is the most contested and that the arc from physiology to long-acting agonists should include drug design.
responses.response: I take the point that a prize for a medicine ought to recognise the person who made the molecule durable, and that Mojsov's claim is the least settled. My disagreement is that the prize category rewards discovery, and the discovery of the active peptide and its insulinotropic action is a necessary step that Knudsen's work builds on. If the committee concludes the priority dispute cannot be resolved, Knudsen is the fallback third name, and I would want that decided in round 2 on evidence rather than on the convenience of a clean story.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks CAR-T (B041) second and TNF blockade (B006) third, and excludes Knudsen from GLP-1 as industrial and translational, supporting Drucker, Holst and Mojsov.
responses.response: We agree on the GLP-1 trio, and I share the view that the discovery component should lead. On CAR-T I am more hesitant than she is: I ranked it sixth because the originators of the chimeric receptor concept are outside the supplied names and solid-tumour efficacy remains unproven, so a June, Sadelain and Rosenberg trio leaves a real attribution hole. TNF blockade I rank higher than most colleagues, but she is right that it relies on a clinical-translational claim that sits awkwardly beside the missing cytokine biology.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response (B014) second as a conceptually clean ER-to-nucleus signalling logic with Mori and Walter as a natural pair, confirmed over thirty years, and ranks optogenetics only fourth as a tool.
responses.response: I agree that B014 is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and that the mechanistic originality is high; I ranked it third myself. I differ on optogenetics: a method that opened causal circuit dissection, including for movement disorders and depression, has precedent for recognition, and I do not think tool status is a demerit. Where he is right is that six credited names make B015 the hardest to configure, so B014 is the safer second prize if the committee prefers a pair without disputed credit.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics (B015) second and proposes Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann, noting that any trio leaves out serious contributors, and puts imatinib (B011) third.
responses.response: I support his trio as the most commonly cited, but I would not let the cap hide the injustice to Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck, and that is exactly why I prefer B027 as the single prize part. On imatinib I rank it eighth: its impact is exceptional, but the credited trio is drug development and clinical proof, with the oncogene discovery outside the credit, which makes the discovery narrative thinner than GLP-1.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for GLP-1(7-36) is strong enough to credit her instead of Knudsen.
Whether a prize that includes the drug-development line would be better framed as a two-part configuration.
Whether Habener's absence from the credited names undermines any GLP-1 configuration in a way the committee should resolve before voting.
Whether B015 can be configured fairly with only three of six credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B027, B015 or B014 from the provided profile. I have roughly twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann, who advocates B014; this does not concern the candidates' own work, but I flag it, and I note that my Greengard postdoctoral connection does not involve any shortlisted candidate. I make no claim of other ties.
